facts.title: Named for the Curies
facts.text: Curium was named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie, the pioneers of radioactivity research. The naming deliberately echoes its lighter chemical cousin gadolinium, which honors the chemist Johan Gadolin, since curium sits directly below gadolinium in the periodic table's structure. It is one of the few elements named after specific people who were themselves scientists.

facts.title: Born in wartime Berkeley
facts.text: Curium was first synthesized in the summer of 1944 by Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, and Albert Ghiorso at the University of California, Berkeley, by bombarding plutonium-239 with alpha particles in a cyclotron. The work was part of the secret Manhattan Project, so the discovery stayed classified for years. Seaborg famously first hinted at the new elements during a children's radio quiz show in 1945 before any formal publication.

facts.title: A metal you can never hold
facts.text: Curium is intensely radioactive, and a sizable sample glows with a soft purple or lilac light in the dark, caused by the energy released as its own radiation excites the surrounding air and the metal itself. The decay is so energetic that a chunk of curium grows noticeably warm to the touch. Handling it requires sealed gloveboxes and remote tools, because even small amounts are dangerous to living tissue.

facts.title: Hotter than its surroundings
facts.text: A single gram of curium-244 releases roughly 3 watts of heat continuously from its radioactive decay, far more thermal power per gram than plutonium-238. This makes curium a candidate fuel for radioisotope thermoelectric generators that could power spacecraft for decades. The intense self-heating is a direct consequence of its short half-life packing a lot of decays into a small time.

facts.title: It explored Mars
facts.text: Curium-244 has served as the alpha-particle source in alpha particle X-ray spectrometers carried aboard NASA Mars rovers, including Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity. The instrument bathes a rock in alpha particles and reads the X-rays that bounce back to identify which elements the rock contains. In a sense, a man-made element helped decode the natural chemistry of another planet.

facts.title: Once thought impossible to separate
facts.text: Curium and its neighbor americium were so chemically similar and so hard to purify that the Berkeley chemists privately nicknamed them pandemonium and delirium during the frustrating separation work. Curium's strong tendency to exist in the +3 oxidation state, like the lanthanides, is exactly what makes it cling to its chemical cousins. Modern ion-exchange techniques finally tamed the separation.

facts.title: A half-life rivaling Earth's age
facts.text: While most curium isotopes vanish quickly, curium-247 has a half-life of about 15.6 million years, and curium-248 lasts roughly 348,000 years. These long-lived forms are valued for research because they stay around long enough to study without constant replenishment. Even the longest-lived curium, though, is far too short-lived to survive from the formation of the solar system to today.

facts.title: Extinct in nature, alive in starlight
facts.text: Curium does not occur naturally on Earth today, but evidence in ancient meteorites suggests curium-247 was present in the early solar system and has since completely decayed away. Astronomers have also detected signs that curium is produced in violent cosmic events such as neutron star mergers, where extreme neutron bombardment builds up heavy elements. So while we make it in reactors, the universe forges it in cataclysms.

facts.title: Seven shifting crystal forms
facts.text: Under increasing pressure, curium metal transforms through several distinct crystal structures, and one of its high-pressure phases is remarkable because its magnetism actively helps stabilize the structure. This is unusual, since magnetism rarely controls the basic atomic arrangement of a metal. Studying these phase changes helps physicists understand how the 5f electrons of the actinides behave under extreme conditions.

facts.title: A stepping stone to heavier elements
facts.text: Curium is not just an endpoint but a launchpad: bombarding curium targets with light ions has been used to create even heavier elements, and curium is itself made by neutron irradiation of plutonium in reactors. Only gram-scale quantities are produced worldwide each year, making it precious and tightly controlled. Its place at atomic number 96 makes it a key rung on the ladder toward the superheavy elements.
